events.text: Lanyon receives a registered letter from Henry Jekyll on the ninth of January.
events.quote: I received by the evening delivery a registered envelope, addressed in the hand of my colleague and old school companion, Henry Jekyll.

events.text: Jekyll begs Lanyon to help him, saying his life and reason are at stake.
events.quote: Lanyon, my life, my honour, my reason, are all at your mercy; if you fail me to-night, I am lost.

events.text: Jekyll orders Poole to wait with a locksmith for Lanyon's arrival.
events.quote: Poole, my butler, has his orders; you will find him waiting your arrival with a locksmith.

events.text: Jekyll instructs Lanyon to force open his cabinet and take the fourth drawer.
events.quote: The door of my cabinet is then to be forced; and you are to go in alone

events.text: Jekyll asks Lanyon to receive a midnight messenger and hand over the drawer.
events.quote: to admit with your own hand into the house a man who will present himself in my name

events.text: Jekyll warns that if the night passes without event, Lanyon has seen the last of him.
events.quote: if that night passes without event, you will know that you have seen the last of Henry Jekyll.

events.text: Lanyon suspects Jekyll is insane but feels bound to obey the appeal.
events.quote: I made sure my colleague was insane; but till that was proved beyond the possibility of doubt, I felt bound to do as he requested.

events.text: Lanyon drives to Jekyll's house, where the butler awaits him.
events.quote: I rose accordingly from table, got into a hansom, and drove straight to Jekyll’s house. The butler was awaiting my arrival

events.text: The carpenter and locksmith work two hours to open Jekyll's cabinet door.
events.quote: after two hour’s work, the door stood open

events.text: Lanyon takes the drawer, has it packed in straw and a sheet, and returns home.
events.quote: I took out the drawer, had it filled up with straw and tied in a sheet, and returned with it to Cavendish Square.

events.text: Lanyon examines the drawer's powders, phial, and book of dated experiments.
events.quote: Here I proceeded to examine its contents.

events.text: Lanyon dismisses his servants and loads an old revolver for self-defence.
events.quote: though I dismissed my servants to bed, I loaded an old revolver, that I might be found in some posture of self-defence

events.text: At midnight a small man knocks gently and crouches against the portico pillars.
events.quote: Twelve o’clock had scarce rung out over London, ere the knocker sounded very gently on the door.

events.text: Lanyon asks if the visitor comes from Dr. Jekyll, and the man gestures yes.
events.quote: “Are you come from Dr. Jekyll?” I asked.

events.text: The visitor glances back at a policeman and hurries inside.
events.quote: There was a policeman not far off, advancing with his bull’s eye open; and at the sight, I thought my visitor started and made greater haste.

events.text: Lanyon sees the visitor clearly for the first time and is struck by his appearance.
events.quote: Here, at last, I had a chance of clearly seeing him. I had never set eyes on him before, so much was certain.

relation_context.story_before_this_passage:
During a Sunday walk, Utterson and Enfield stop at a sinister door. Enfield recalls Hyde trampling a girl, then paying her family £100 with a genuine cheque. Utterson studies Jekyll’s will, which leaves everything to Hyde if Jekyll vanishes. Lanyon says Jekyll grew too fanciful and has never heard of Hyde. Keeping watch, Utterson accosts Hyde, who admits Jekyll is out, gives a Soho address, then snarls and disappears inside. Poole confirms Hyde has a key and all servants must obey him. Jekyll pales when Utterson mentions Hyde, refuses more, but says he can be rid of Hyde whenever he chooses. He asks Utterson to help Hyde for his sake when gone.

A maid saw Hyde cane Sir Danvers Carew to death. The mangled body bore a sealed envelope for Utterson, who identified Carew. Inspector Newcomen showed the broken stick, which Utterson recognized as Jekyll’s gift. They searched Hyde’s rooms, finding the other half and a burnt cheque book. Hyde had thousands at the bank, but few familiars, no photograph, and wildly differing descriptions.

Poole admits Utterson to Jekyll’s cabinet. Jekyll swears he will never see Hyde again. Jekyll gives Utterson a letter signed Edward Hyde, saying he burned the envelope, which had no postmark, and that Hyde dictated his will. Poole says no letter came except by post. Guest finds the murderer’s letter identical to Jekyll’s note. Utterson locks it in his safe, suspecting forgery.

After the murder, Hyde vanishes and rewards are offered. Jekyll resumes old friendships, then shuts his door; Poole says he is confined. Utterson finds Lanyon decayed, doomed, refusing Jekyll’s name. [P17] “Why don’t you read it, sir?” asked Poole.
[P18] “Because I fear,” replied the lawyer solemnly. “God grant I have no cause for it!” And with that he brought the paper to his eyes and read as follows:
[P19] “My dear Utterson,—When this shall fall into your hands, I shall have disappeared, under what circumstances I have not the penetration to foresee, but my instinct and all the circumstances of my nameless situation tell me that the end is sure and must be early. Go then, and first read the narrative which Lanyon warned me he was to place in your hands; and if you care to hear more, turn to the confession of
[P20] “Your unworthy and unhappy friend,
[P21] “HENRY JEKYLL.”
[P22] “There was a third enclosure?” asked Utterson.
[P23] “Here, sir,” said Poole, and gave into his hands a considerable packet sealed in several places.
[P24] The lawyer put it in his pocket. “I would say nothing of this paper. If your master has fled or is dead, we may at least save his credit. It is now ten; I must go home and read these documents in quiet; but I shall be back before midnight, when we shall send for the police.”
[P25] They went out, locking the door of the theatre behind them; and Utterson, once more leaving the servants gathered about the fire in the hall, trudged back to his office to read the two narratives in which this mystery was now to be explained.

known_before.name: Dr. Lanyon
known_before.tagline: Utterson's old friend and fellow doctor
known_before.bio: Dr. Lanyon is a doctor with a house in Cavendish Square, an old friend of Utterson and formerly of Dr. Jekyll. He is boisterous, decided and theatrical but genuine. Over ten years ago he judged Jekyll too fanciful and wrong in mind. When Utterson asked about Hyde, Lanyon had never heard of him. He dined with Jekyll and Utterson as inseparable friends, but later Utterson found him visibly decayed; Lanyon declared himself a doomed man who would never recover, refused to hear Jekyll's name and called him dead to him.

Lanyon takes to his bed and dies within a fortnight.

He is tall and well built, known for charities and religion, but has become fanciful and estranged from Dr. Lanyon.
